title: Finite-message characterization of private-coin complexity
statement: Let $f : X \to Y \to \alpha$ be a function, let $\varepsilon \in \bbr$ be an error bound, and let $n \in \bbn$. Then the $\varepsilon$-error private-coin randomized communication complexity satisfies $R_\varepsilon(f) \le n$ if and only if there exist coin-tape lengths $n_X, n_Y \in \bbn$ and a private-coin finite-message protocol $p$ with randomness spaces $\{0,1\}^{n_X}$ and $\{0,1\}^{n_Y}$ (over input types $X$, $Y$ and output type $\alpha$) such that $p$ computes $f$ with error at most $\varepsilon$ on every input pair and has worst-case communication cost at most $n$. Thus the private-coin complexity, defined via binary-message protocols, is unchanged when one instead allows protocols whose players may send elements of arbitrary finite nonempty message alphabets, each $\beta$-valued message being charged $\lceil \log_2 \abs{\beta} \rceil$ bits.
hypotheses_covered: existence of coin-tape lengths n_X, n_Y
existence of a private-coin finite-message protocol p over those coin tapes
p ε-computes f (error ≤ ε on every input pair)
replaced:
For any $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $R_\varepsilon(f) \le n$ if and only if there exist coin-tape sizes
$n_X, n_Y \in \mathbb{N}$ and a \emph{finite-message} protocol
$p : \mathrm{FiniteMessage.Protocol}(\{0,1\}^{n_X}, \{0,1\}^{n_Y}, X, Y, \alpha)$ such that
$p$ $\varepsilon$-approximately computes $f$ and $p.\mathrm{complexity} \le n$.
This establishes that passing to the finite-message variant does not change the complexity measure.
